# 4 Maccabees Chapter 1 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal)
**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Greek MS (Codex Sinaiticus) | **Section:** Philosophical Introduction

---

**1** The subject I am about to discuss is most philosophical: whether devout reason is sovereign over the passions. I strongly urge you to give your earnest attention to philosophy.

**2** For the question is essential to every person, and beyond that it produces the highest commendation for those devoted to philosophy — namely whether reason is master over the passions.

**3** But we must first determine what reason is, what passion is, how many forms passion takes, and whether reason rules all of them.

**4** Reason is the mind that chooses the life of wisdom with right deliberation.

**5** And wisdom is the knowledge of things divine and human, together with an understanding of their causes.

**6** This wisdom is imparted through the education of the law, by means of which we learn divine matters reverently and human matters to our profit.

**7** The forms of wisdom are prudence, justice, courage, and temperance.

**8** Prudence is the most authoritative of all, for through it reason exercises control over the passions.

**9** Among the passions, pleasure and pain are the two most comprehensive; and each of these belongs naturally to both soul and body.

**10** There are many emotional conditions that attend both pleasure and pain.

**11** Desire precedes pleasure, and joy follows after it.

**12** Fear precedes pain, and grief follows after it.

**13** Anger is a passion that combines pleasure and pain, as one who reflects will recognize.

**14** Within pleasure there exists also an evil disposition, which is the most multifaceted of all the passions.

**15** Among the passions of the soul are arrogance, love of money, desire for honor, quarrelsomeness, envy, and malice.

**16** Among the passions of the body are gluttony, greed, and the desire for solitary pleasures.

**17** Reason, I maintain, is the guide of the virtues and the sovereign over the passions.

**18** Observe through those things that impede temperance that reason is indeed sovereign over the passions.

**19** For temperance consists in mastering the appetites.

**20** Some appetites belong to the soul and some to the body, and reason appears to hold mastery over both.

**21** Otherwise, when we are drawn toward forbidden foods, how is it that we turn away from the pleasure they would bring? Is it not that reason is able to govern the appetites?

**22** I believe it is. Therefore when we desire seafood and birds and four-footed animals and all the foods forbidden to us by the law, we abstain from them through the mastery of reason.

**23** For the appetitive passions are restrained and curbed by the temperate mind, and all the impulses of the body are held in check by reason.

**24** And what is more, reason is able to overcome even pain through the virtue of courage.

**25** How does this come about? Because a person holds to the love of wisdom. Thus even when the body is weakened by age or illness, reason retains its authority over it.

**26** I shall now demonstrate this through the examples of Eleazar and the seven brothers and their mother.

**27** All of these, by despising their sufferings even to the point of death, demonstrated that reason governs the passions.

**28** I am right to praise these men and that woman who died with them for their virtues, and to call them blessed for their courage and endurance, and to consider them admirable for overcoming their passions — admired not only by people in general but even by their torturers.

**29** They became the cause of the overthrow of tyranny over their nation, having conquered the tyrant by their patient endurance, so that through them their homeland was purified.

**30** I shall now enter upon the full discussion of the matter. As is my custom, I begin by stating my theme, and then I shall proceed to the narrative, giving glory to the all-wise God.

**31** The question is therefore whether reason is sovereign over the passions.

**32** We shall determine what true reason is: it is the mind that chooses, with wise deliberation, the life of wisdom.

**33** Wisdom is imparted through the law's instruction, and through it we learn divine things reverently and human things advantageously.

**34** The forms of wisdom are prudence, justice, courage, and temperance.

**35** The most commanding of these is prudence, by which reason alone rules over the passions.
